sections.preamble: You are an expert coding assistant operating inside pi, a coding agent harness. You help users by reading files, executing commands, editing code, and writing new files.
sections.tools:
<tools>
- read: Read file contents
- bash: Execute bash commands (ls, grep, find, etc.)
- edit: Make precise file edits with exact text replacement, including multiple disjoint edits in one call
- write: Create or overwrite files

In addition to the tools above, you may have access to other custom tools depending on the project.
</tools>
sections.rules:
<rules>
- Use bash for file operations like ls, rg, find
- Use read to examine files instead of cat or sed.
- You can inspect PI_* environment variables for current model and session details.
- Use edit for precise changes (edits[].oldText must match exactly)
- When changing multiple separate locations in one file, use one edit call with multiple entries in edits[] instead of multiple edit calls
- Each edits[].oldText is matched against the original file, not after earlier edits are applied. Do not emit overlapping or nested edits. Merge nearby changes into one edit.
- Keep edits[].oldText as small as possible while still being unique in the file. Do not pad with large unchanged regions.
- Use write only for new files or complete rewrites.
- Be concise in your responses
- Show file paths clearly when working with files
</rules>

content.text:
Make a website that, if everyone saw and used it, would improve the world for the greatest number of people.

Build this as an interactive web page in the current directory.
- The entry point is index.html. Put your code in JavaScript ES modules loaded from it
  (`<script type="module" src="main.js">`), and add a short README.md.
- You may use npm packages: `npm install <package>` here, then import them by name
  (`import * as THREE from "three"`). No CDN URLs and no import maps.
- Afterwards the page is packaged into one self-contained index.html with esbuild: every script and
  stylesheet index.html references is bundled with everything it imports. Load assets the page needs
  with `import` (they become data URLs) or generate them in code, never by URL string.
- The packaged page runs offline in a sandboxed iframe: no network requests, and no localStorage,
  cookies or other storage (they throw there).
- Check that it packages: `esbuild main.js --bundle --format=esm --outfile=/dev/null` must succeed.
  Don't build or package the page yourself; that happens afterwards.
- To look at the page yourself, serve it locally and screenshot it in headless Chrome (Chrome is
  installed, and a driver such as puppeteer-core or playwright can be npm-installed here). Save every
  screenshot you look at as a .jpg file, never .png: each image you read stays in your context, and a
  long session of large .png files can hit the provider's per-request image limit and end the run.
- Only create or edit files inside the current directory.
- Finish with a short summary of what you built.

The author finalized the flag for forgiveness and "are we okay," warning that a plea asks the other to close their pain. They also added flags for "you should" and "have you tried," since advice-y drafts are common.

The author decided to keep the flag list tight at ten entries so the tool feels precise rather than naggy. They will add a positive reinforcement note that appears when no flags trigger, ensuring users do not feel policed. An optional less-power sentence and a grief path that bypasses the composer were also planned.

A print stylesheet is being added to strip the header, footer, and shadow for clean card printing. The speak view will keep its header and footer readable. A subtle paper texture vignette with a warm top highlight is also being added so screenshots do not look flat.

The paper texture now uses two radial gradients for subtle depth. A flex layout with `min-height: 100vh` will keep short pages from looking like a strip at the top. The author is also considering whether the home page doors should expand to fill the viewport.

A decorative stitch will sit between the home page lede and doors for visual breathing room. The author is now drafting the five core files: content.js, style.css, main.js, index.html, and README.md. To keep the build manageable, main.js will stay under 800 lines and content.js under 700, with render logic consolidated into one file.

main.js will export nothing and run as a side-effect entry point. The init function sets the default route to #home, listens for hash changes and global events, then renders the initial view. A keyboard handler is being drafted.

The keyboard handler now ignores input fields and routes the 1, 2, and 3 keys to the corresponding line buttons. Choosing a line stores the selection in state and renders the choice view. In choice mode, the consequence section scrolls into view automatically.

The `next-beat` action now advances the scene by recording the chosen option, clearing the selection, incrementing the beat index, and re-rendering. When the beat list is exhausted, the view falls back to a close screen. The retry action resets the choice and returns to the route view.

Retry will scroll to the options section. The near page drill state will store a daily choice and reset when the day changes. Drill HTML will be generated from `drillForToday()`, with a note shown below the selection.

A "Another situation" button will cycle through the four daily drills using a `state.drillOffset` counter. The author is now ready to compose the full content and code.

A five-word mnemonic—Steady, Fact, Own, Hear, One—will sit directly under the home page thesis so even a brief visit teaches something. A short link to the five moves and a card option will sit below it. If the layout feels crowded, the author will move the mnemonic into the doors area.

The author abandoned the tall single-column home layout. A two-column grid will place the headline, lede, and mnemonic on the left and the three doors on the right. This keeps the page under 900 pixels and looks more intentional than a centered blog.

The door CSS is now complete. The last door gets a bottom border. Titles use a serif typeface at 1.85rem with tight letter spacing. Descriptions are italic and muted. Number badges are small and brown. Hovering the door creates a subtle gold gradient.

**Mend** is a small practice for the minute after something breaks. If people used it, ordinary life would be less cruel, and more preventable harm would actually get stopped.

It works at three distances:

- **Here** means naming the state you are in, then using a physiological sigh, before you speak or send anything.
- **Near** means repairing what you broke, or staying with someone who is hurting. Scenes show why “but,” “sorry you feel,” and “just a joke” widen a break. It also says plainly when an apology is the wrong tool.
- **Far** means giving blood if you can, money toward suffering that is common and measurable, and the skill itself to one other person.

**The words** turns a real situation into something you can say, and flags the phrases that undo it. **In danger** is always one click away, for you or for someone else. Nothing is stored. Nothing is sent.
